findings.statement: The expansion associated with Axayácatl (1469–1481) includes sculpted serpent heads, an Altar of Frogs on Tláloc's north side, and a Coyolxauhqui replica at Huitzilopochtli's south stair.
findings.what_to_look_for: Look for serpent heads, frog altar and a replica (not original) monolith

findings.statement: The earliest excavated temple phase preserves colored walls at Tláloc's shrine and a painted Chac-Mool near its entrance; the Huitzilopochtli side includes a téchcatl ritual stone.
findings.what_to_look_for: Inspect original paint remnants and distinguish ritual interpretation from stone evidence

findings.statement: The Casa de las Águilas was built and enlarged three times during c.1430–1500; three rooms are visible, others lie beneath Justo Sierra Street. Interior benches bear processions and two ceramic eagle-warrior figures were found there.
findings.what_to_look_for: Identify column bases, benches and sculpted eagle-head stair elements

findings.statement: Several superimposed floor surfaces in the north patio are associated by INAH with subsidence and flooding. Phase VI Building B, the tzompantli altar, is decorated with stone-carved human skulls.
findings.what_to_look_for: Compare successive paving levels and sculpture; dates/cause need original report

findings.statement: A brick drain installed around 1900 beneath present Guatemala Street sliced across Templo Mayor's successive building phases in a strip about two metres wide.
findings.locator: Etapa IV y V > Colector de agua
findings.what_to_look_for: Find brick collector under metal walkway

findings.statement: Utility workers exposed the Coyolxauhqui stone at Argentina and Guatemala on 21 February 1978, leading to Proyecto Templo Mayor; the museum opened in 1987.
findings.what_to_look_for: Original sculpture in museum versus replica at temple stair; 1978 event may duplicate legacy claims

findings.statement: Four cathedral-atrial archaeological windows show walls tentatively assigned to side chapels and sacristy of a 1525 church commissioned by Cortés, likely completed c.1532 and demolished in 1626.
findings.what_to_look_for: Four atrium windows; specific wall identifications tentative

findings.statement: The 4.0 × 2.2 m atrium window displays colonial tezontle-and-mud masonry with lime-sand plaster and red paint; beneath lie walls and a possibly Mexica flagstone floor.
findings.locator: Ventana 1, second and third descriptive paragraphs
findings.what_to_look_for: Compare layered colonial wall and lower pavement; possible Mexica attribution

findings.statement: Excavations during 1975–76 underpinning exposed two phases of a north talud wall assigned to the Mexica Templo del Sol. Tezontle and andesite were mud-set beneath lime-sand-volcanic aggregate stucco.
findings.locator: Sagrario, excavations 1975–76 and first-window material description
findings.what_to_look_for: See lower basement windows; original field report not yet inspected

findings.statement: The second Sagrario window exposes a painted solar-disk pink-andesite plaque with four chalchihuite corner designs, beside wooden foundation piles of the 1749–1768 Sagrario.
findings.locator: Sagrario, second-window carved plaque and northwest corner
findings.what_to_look_for: Look for plaque's colors and colonial wooden piles; interpretations may need corroboration

findings.statement: A 12 × 4 m archaeological window at the Second Patio Mariano reveals three construction phases of a pre-Hispanic stair, with five andesite-block steps in the latest phase and earlier basalt-slab foundations.
findings.locator: Palacio Nacional Ventana 1, final descriptive paragraph
findings.what_to_look_for: Identify five steps and distinct layers

findings.statement: A 3.5 × 1.6 m window excavated in 2003–2004 contains a balustraded stair linking plaza to Mexica shrine. Attribution to a Tezcatlipoca complex remains a hypothesis.
findings.what_to_look_for: Observe stair, orientation and explicit uncertainty about temple dedication

findings.statement: A 6 × 4 m Palace excavation exposes pre-Hispanic stair, ceramic-tube drains, stone pavement and cruciform column support, plus later tezontle drain; the column's association with Cortés's residence is interpretive.
findings.what_to_look_for: Locate separate drainage phases and the column base

findings.statement: Cortés occupied the former Casas Nuevas of Moctezuma after conquest; his heirs sold the property to the Crown in 1562 for viceregal and Audiencia use; after independence in 1821 the site became Palacio Nacional.
findings.what_to_look_for: Distinguish successive Indigenous, colonial and national political uses

inspection_limitations: No full original excavation monograph inspected in this run
Some interpretations explicitly tentative (Palace Tezcatlipoca; cathedral early walls; 1978 discovery may duplicate legacy records)
